column1: i,s|Feel vowel and consonant airflow|Sustain the vowel in seat; then sustain its first sound. Locate the narrowing.|Which has a narrow hiss?|The consonant|The vowel
i,eɪ|Steady or moving vowel|Hold the vowel of seat, then lengthen sale. Notice whether the tongue changes position.|Which has a glide?|sale|seat
i,u|Explore front and back|Move slowly from the vowel in seat to food with a mirror or a hand near your lips.|Which begins farther forward in the mouth?|seat|food

i,u|Separate tongue from lip movement|Keep the lips as still as is comfortable while you move between the two tongue positions. Restore normal lip shape and compare.|What are you trying to isolate?|Tongue movement|Loudness

ɪ,ʊ|Find an intermediate position|Slide from a close front vowel toward a close back one. Stop halfway and notice that the result need not be an English word.|Which can change without changing pitch?|Vowel quality|The note you sing
i,æ|Discover vertical movement|Alternate seat and bad slowly. Touch the outside of your jaw to notice the change.|Which target generally needs a more open mouth?|bad|seat
ɛ,æ|Pause between two heights|Glide from bed toward bad, pausing between them. Return to the original word.|What makes the contrast here?|Vowel openness|Adding an extra consonant
i,ɛ,æ,u,ʊ,ə|Tour the steady vowels|For each model, name one physical change before trying the next vowel. Return to your first sound from memory.|Which is a steady vowel in this set?|/ɛ/|/eɪ/
æ,i|Watch the jaw|Alternate the vowels in pack and peak in a mirror. Look away and reproduce the contrast by feel.|Which word usually opens the jaw farther?|pack|peak

i,ɑ|Connect height and openness|Trace a vertical line from close to open while changing your vowel. Notice what happens to the jaw.|What usually accompanies greater openness?|A lower jaw|A tighter lip closure
æ,ə|Compare jaw effort|Say bad, release toward a relaxed central vowel, and repeat with less effort.|Which target is typically more relaxed here?|schwa|The open vowel in bad
u,i|Observe the lips|Mute your voice and form the two vowels; then add voice and check the visible difference.|Which has rounded lips?|food|seat
ʊ,ɛ|Spread and round|Move the corners of the lips gradually from spread to rounded. Listen before looking at the chart.|What changed most visibly?|Lip shape|Vocal-fold vibration
u,oʊ|Move the lips forward|Say go, exaggerating the forward motion once; repeat comfortably in a phrase.|Which part of go can show increasing rounding?|The end|A separate consonant after the vowel

i,u|Try the opposite rounding|Attempt a familiar vowel with its unusual lip shape. Release back to the reference and describe the change.|Why use the unusual shape?|To notice the contribution of the lips|To memorize it as the standard model

i,ɪ|Change duration on purpose|Sustain sit and shorten seat without intentionally changing the vowel quality. Record both.|What alone cannot reliably distinguish the two vowels?|Duration|The combined vowel cues
i,u,ɑ,ɔ,ɝ|Explore length across vowels|Sustain each target comfortably, then place it in a short word. Compare the reference accent labels.|Which notation marks length in a British transcription?|ː|ˈ
i|Compare vowel timing in matched frames|Say bead and beat at a steady pace. Listen to the vowel before the final consonant.|Which context often allows a longer vowel?|Before d|Before t
i,ɪ|Reverse habitual lengths|Try a deliberately brief seat and prolonged sit, then return to natural versions.|Which change did you deliberately control?|Timing|Word spelling

æ|Compare different environments|Say bad, bag and back on a steady beat. Listen for how the following sound influences the vowel.|Which is a fair comparison?|Same speaking pace|One word whispered and one shouted
æ|Listen around the vowel in bad|Compare bat and bad in two requests. Notice the vowel and the ending together.|Which pairs with a usually longer vowel?|bad|bat

i,ɛ,æ,ʊ,u|Navigate the vowel map|Trace a route across the chart and back. Close the chart and name two changes along the way.|What does the vertical direction roughly represent?|Vowel openness|Word frequency

eɪ,aɪ,ɔɪ|Find a shared glide destination|Say day, my and toy slowly. Compare where the tongue moves near the end.|What do the three glides share?|Movement toward a closer front position|The same starting vowel
aɪ,eɪ|Feel the front glide|Hold the beginning of ride, then complete it in one syllable. Repeat with late.|How many syllables does the moving vowel need?|One|Two
oʊ,aʊ|Find a rounded destination|Alternate coat and loud. Notice how the lips change near the end.|What can both vowels do near the end?|Become more rounded|Close into a stop
aʊ,oʊ|Isolate the rounded glide|Mime the last part of now and go, then add voice without adding a second beat.|What stays continuous?|The vowel movement|A series of separate stops
aʊ,oʊ|Distinguish starting positions|Imagine two routes that finish with rounding. Compare the first instant of now and no.|Which starts more open?|now|no

ɪɹ,ɛɹ,ʊɹ|Read British centring vowels|Hear the British references, then the American r-colored equivalents. Identify the change expected in each model.|Which is an American ending in near?|A vowel moving into r|A required silent final consonant
aɪ|Time the glide|Say ride and write at a similar pace. Shorten the whole glide while keeping one syllable.|Which often has a shorter glide?|write|ride

eɪ|Keep one beat through a glide|Say sale on a hand tap and listen for a single syllable. Avoid adding a second beat at the end.|Where does the main energy of the glide begin?|Toward its starting position|After a separate second syllable
ɔɪ,aʊ|Read visible glide clues|Mime toy and town. Observe which direction the lips change, then verify by speaking.|Which glide releases initial rounding?|toy|town
m,ɑ|Identify closure and openness|Hum m and slowly open to a vowel. Compare airflow even when both sounds are voiced.|Which has a complete lip closure?|m|The vowel
f,v,s,z|Switch voice on and off|Hold f and add voice to make v. Repeat with s and z, keeping the mouth shape steady.|Which pair shares lip–teeth contact?|f and v|s and v
p,b|Compare stop strength|Alternate pin and bin. Observe the release, aspiration and vibration rather than relying on one cue.|Which may have a puff when stressed initially?|pin|bin

t,d|Experiment with effort|Say ten with a weaker release and den with a stronger one. Compare with each normal reference.|What is the purpose of this reversal?|Notice several cues to a contrast|Make every voiced sound louder
p,t,k|Trace three stop closures|Say pin, tin and kin. Identify the closure before releasing the vowel.|Which uses the back of the tongue?|kin|pin
t,tʃ|Stop or affricate|Compare ten and chin. Slow the beginning without inserting an extra vowel.|Which releases into prolonged friction?|chin|ten
p,t,k,tʃ|Locate closures without a diagram|Mime the stops from lips to back of tongue. Then find the start of chin.|Which closure is at the lips?|p|k
f,s,ʃ,θ|Sustain four fricatives|Hold each beginning without the vowel. Notice a different narrow passage for the air.|Which group permits continuing friction?|f, s, sh|p, t, k
f,θ,s,ʃ|Move friction backward|Compare fine, thin, sip and ship. Name the contact or narrowing for each sound.|Where is the narrowing for f?|Lower lip and upper teeth|Two closed lips
m,l,ɹ,w,j|Compare resonant consonants|Sustain what you can of the initial movement and identify which sounds glide into a vowel.|Which pair glides quickly toward a vowel?|w and y in yes|p and t
m,n,ŋ|Move a nasal closure|Hum m, n and ng. Keep voice on while the closure travels backward.|Which closure is farthest back?|ng|m
h|Shape breath for the next vowel|Whisper he and ha, then add voice to the vowels. Notice the breath already shaped for what follows.|What shapes the initial breath here?|The coming vowel|A lip seal
l|Let air past the tongue sides|Hold the first sound of lane. Keep the tongue tip in contact and let air pass laterally.|Which best describes the contact?|Tip at the ridge|Both lips sealed
ɹ|Explore an r shape|Try a comfortable r in red without tapping the tongue tip. Replay rain and lane.|Which contrast are you exploring?|r and l|m and n
w,j|Compare two glides|Whisper wet and yet. Observe where each glide begins before the vowel.|Which starts with lip rounding?|wet|yet
w|Release from rounded lips|Mime west then speak it. Avoid touching the lip to the teeth.|Which contact would move it toward v?|Lip against teeth|Rounding alone
j|Glide from a high front position|Begin with a short ee-like position and move directly into yes. Keep it one syllable.|Which begins with the target consonant?|yet|jet
ɹ,w,j|Listen to linking transitions|Compare go out, see it and a British far away. Identify the different movements across vowels.|Which may have a j-like transition?|see it|go out

i,clusters|Blend symbols into a word|Build seat one sound at a time, then say it in a single movement. Repeat with a fresh word.|What should disappear as you blend?|Breaks between sounds|The final consonant

link|Notice neighboring movements|Say take separately and inside take a seat. Notice how the next vowel changes the release.|Which should remain recoverable?|The intended word|Identical timing in both versions
rhythm|Change speed on the chart|Tap a short phrase slowly, then normally, keeping the same sequence and main beat.|What can shorten at natural speed?|Unstressed material|Every stressed vowel equally
stress|Use breath for a beat|Say the noun record on one comfortable breath. Tap the first syllable and release the second.|Which syllable leads the noun?|First|Second
longstress|Locate stress before repeating|Say technique and transfer it to a sentence. Preserve its main beat at normal speed.|What carries the main stress?|nique|tech
ə,weak|Release energy in light syllables|Say about, then place it in a sentence. Keep the first vowel relaxed.|Which syllable can reduce?|The first|The stressed second syllable
family|Distinguish primary and secondary stress|Mark the two levels in photographic. Say it slowly and naturally.|Which mark shows secondary stress?|ˌ|ˈ

stress|Shift stress to change the reading|Put record into noun and verb contexts. Change the beat before recording again.|Which reading suits “record this”?|Second-syllable stress|First-syllable stress
family|Trace a derivative family|Compare photograph and photography. Mark where the strongest beat moves.|Does adding syllables always preserve the original stress?|No|Yes

longstress|Notice pitch at the main beat|Say develop with the main beat on vel. Change pitch while keeping the word recognizable.|Which can contribute to word stress?|Pitch movement|Capital letters in a recording

reduction|Notice assimilation|Say green bag carefully and then fluidly. Observe whether the tongue anticipates the lips of b.|What influences the final sound of green?|The following lip closure|The spelling of green
reduction|Notice an omitted closure|Compare next week at two speeds. Keep the plan clear while changing the cluster.|Which consonant may be difficult to hear?|t in next|w in week
weak|Relax an unstressed vowel|Compare strong and weak to in an invitation. Try the lighter form in a whole phrase.|Which symbol is common in the reduced form?|ə|aɪ

aɪ,weak|Shorten a glide in unstressed speech|Say my on its own and in my bag with the beat on bag. Compare how fully the glide develops.|Which reading favors a shorter my?|Unstressed before bag|A correction focused on MY
weak|Choose strong or weak forms by meaning|Offer to drive, then correct a doubt. Keep the same words and move the beat.|When correcting ability, which word stands out?|can|drive
link|Hear speech across spaces|Say pick it up without three separate starts. Tap the written boundaries as you listen.|Does every written space need silence?|No|Yes

ɪɹ|Explore linking r in British speech|Compare the end of near alone with near it in a non-rhotic reading. Contrast your American model.|Where can linking r appear in the British reading?|Before the next vowel|Only before silence

ɛɹ|Recognize an added r transition|In a British listening context, compare the idea alone and the idea of it. Explore a possible r transition before of.|Which describes intrusive r?|A possible transition without written r|A compulsory sound in every accent
w|Notice rounded transitions between vowels|Say go in slowly, then at normal speed. Feel the lips travel between the vowels.|Which glide-like transition may occur?|w|j
j|Notice front transitions between vowels|Say see Anna in one group. Avoid stopping abruptly after see.|Which glide-like transition may occur?|j|w
link,w,j,ɹ|Compare linking mechanisms|Say turn it, go out, see it and far away. Classify one transition in each.|Which links a final consonant to a vowel?|turn it|go out

group|Hear word boundaries within a stream|Record a nice day and an ice day. Shift the boundary and use context to help the listener.|What can change while sounds remain similar?|The lexical grouping|The audio file format

emphasis|Distinguish word stress from sentence focus|Say a stressed word in two sentences, only one with main focus on it.|What can move with the speaker's intention?|Sentence prominence|The word's spelling

rhythm|Fit light words between beats|Tap bus and nine in two phrases of different lengths. Fit the shorter words comfortably.|What may compress between beats?|Unstressed syllables|The meaning of the time

syllables,rhythm|Contrast two rhythm patterns|Say a line with equal syllable beats and then with selected prominent words. Compare.|Which version can help key details stand out?|Selective prominence|Equal emphasis everywhere
rhythm|Listen before tapping|Listen to the model once without text. On replay tap only the beats you hear.|What should guide the taps?|Heard prominence|Every written letter
weak|Reduce words in a group|Say a short offer and let its function words recede. Compare with a version stressing every word.|Which often becomes light in a neutral offer?|can|The new action

emphasis|Change meaning with one focus shift|Record I sent the note twice. Correct the person in one take and the item in the other.|What changes between your takes?|The corrected detail|The dictionary meaning of note

given|Find the tonic syllable|Listen to an answer about a meeting. Mark the syllable carrying the main pitch change.|Which detail often carries the tonic?|The new or contrasted detail|Always the first word
checking|Control pitch direction and range|Say really with a rise, a fall and a smaller pitch range. Replay all three.|Which pair differs in direction?|Rise versus fall|High versus low starting pitch
given|Hear the tail after the tonic|Say NINA came on Monday with the main movement on Nina. Listen to the rest of the group.|Which part follows the tonic?|The tail|The onset

rhythm|Find where the prominent part begins|Add a light lead-in before the first prominent syllable and compare both versions.|What is the onset here?|The first prominent syllable in the group|The final consonant
asking|Name a pitch movement|Trace a rise, a fall and a fall-rise with your hand. Say a confirmation in two versions.|Which label describes going down and then up?|Fall-rise|Level

attitude|Hear attitude within a situation|Say sure once as encouragement and once as a doubtful check. Listen in context.|What helps interpret the tone?|The situation and words together|Pitch direction alone
asking|Try more than one question tune|Ask about an address, then repeat as a tentative check. Keep the grammar unchanged.|Can a grammatically complete question have a falling tune?|Yes|No
given|Present shared and new information|Name a known place, then add the new time. Make the difference audible in groups.|Which detail needs presenting as new?|The time|The already agreed place
quote|Signal whose voice is speaking|Introduce a quotation, switch voice for it and return to narration.|What can signal the switch?|Pitch range and grouping|Spelling the quote aloud

continue|Try level tone while holding a turn|Pause on a relatively level pitch during a list, then finish the final item.|What might level delivery signal here?|A turn in progress|A universal rule of agreement

topic|Reset the pitch range at a new topic|End one idea, then introduce a new topic higher in your range. Keep it comfortable.|What does a pitch reset help mark?|A new stretch of discourse|An extra syllable
